findings.title: Cleanup logs use Error level and log nil error on success
findings.body: Lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579 use r.log.Error(...) for routine cleanup progress messages (e.g. 'Annotations to clean by time', 'cleaned tags'). The function already returns early on a non-nil error, so when execution reaches these log statements the err value is always nil, yet it is still passed as the 'err' key. The result is that every successful cleanup cycle emits Error-level log records containing a nil error. Combined with the cleanup ticker being moved to 1 minute in cleanup.go, this means an Error-level log is emitted on every pass of the cleanup job, polluting error monitoring and breaking any alerting/log filters that assume Error level indicates a real failure. The level should be Debug or Info, and the 'err' key should only be logged when non-nil (or moved into the error branch). Existing call sites in the same package use r.log.Info for routine ops (line 410: 'delete') and cleanup.go uses Debug for normal results (line 129), so this is also inconsistent with surrounding code.

findings.title: Cleanup ticker shortened from 10m to 1m without justification
findings.body: The Run loop's ticker was changed from time.Minute * 10 to time.Minute * 1. This is a 10x increase in cleanup job frequency that is unrelated to the deadlock fix described in the PR (which is in xorm_store.go). The change is not mentioned in the PR description and is bundled with the deadlock fix. With a 9 minute per-job timeout (line 89) and now a 1 minute tick, a slow cleanup cycle (e.g. while there are many annotations to remove) will cause the next tick to fire while clean(ctx) is still executing, leading to overlapping clean() invocations on the same shared parent context. This risk is amplified by the new 'fetchIDs then deleteByIDs' pattern, which performs two DB roundtrips per batch instead of one. The ticker value should either be reverted to 10 minutes or justified/handled separately, and the loop should track whether a clean cycle is in progress to avoid concurrent runs.

findings.title: SQL and parameters are passed as separate args to session.Exec
findings.body:
In deleteByIDs, the call is:

    res, err := session.Exec(append([]any{sql}, args...)...)

The first element of the variadic args slice is the statement text and the remaining elements are the bind parameters. xorm's Session.Exec expects (sql string, args ...interface{}); passing the SQL string as a positional argument via the args slice is unusual and depends on undocumented behavior of the dialect's Exec wrapper. Several xorm code paths treat the first element as a parameter and prepend the SQL separately, which can lead to the SQL being interpreted as part of the parameter list (e.g. on PostgreSQL where the driver receives the SQL as a query string only when calling Exec(sql, args...) directly). This should be called as session.Exec(sql, args...) to match the rest of the file (e.g. line 415, 419, 426, 430) and avoid silently malforming the query on some drivers.

findings.title: cleanupWHERE clause is built from annotationType without an AND before created filter
findings.body:
The condition built for the MaxAge branch is:

    cond := fmt.Sprintf(`%s AND created < %v ORDER BY id DESC %s`, annotationType, cutoffDate, r.db.GetDialect().Limit(...))

The annotationType argument (e.g. 'alert_id > 0 AND dashboard_id > 0' for dashboard annotations, or 'alert_id = 0 AND dashboard_id = 0' for API annotations) is concatenated directly. If any caller passes a type filter that ends with OR rather than AND, the trailing 'AND created <' will silently change the operator precedence. More importantly, the MaxCount branch builds:

    cond := fmt.Sprintf(`%s ORDER BY id DESC %s`, annotationType, r.db.GetDialect().LimitOffset(...))

without any check that annotationType contains a WHERE fragment rather than a full clause. The comment in the code refers to annotationType as 'e.g. alert_id > 0 AND dashboard_id > 0', but the function silently trusts the caller. There is no validation, and an accidental empty string would produce 'SELECT id FROM annotation  ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT N', which would happily walk the entire annotation table per batch (and there is no OFFSET/limit on the SELECT itself other than what the dialect appends). A guard against empty annotationType or a small comment/contract would make this safer.

findings.title: Integration tests now skipped under -short with no unit-level coverage added
findings.body: TestAnnotationCleanUp and TestOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst were renamed to TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp / TestIntegrationOldAnnotationsAreDeletedFirst and both gained a testing.Short() skip. These were the only tests that exercised CleanAnnotations / CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags in any way. They required a real DB before too, but now they run in zero CI configurations that use -short, and the deadlock regression that this PR fixes has no unit-test coverage of its own. There should be at least one non-DB unit test that exercises the new helpers (e.g. that untilDoneOrCancelled terminates on ctx.Done() and on zero affected rows, and that deleteByIDs short-circuits on an empty id list), so the new code paths are exercised in short mode and refactoring does not silently break them.
